extracted.subtask_description: AP wire news dispatches reporting on international military and political events (Indochina, Korea) and related U.S. congressional hearings; mixes battlefield reporting, analysis, and legal/procedural explanation. Typical audience is readers seeking current-events reporting and background on policy and legal implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone recording disclosure requirement (Federal Communications Act of 1934)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a call is recorded it cannot be made public without the consent of the party on the other end of the line. The Act does not make the act of recording illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney Ray Jenkins summarized the legal situation: monitoring/recording itself is not a violation of the law, but divulging a recorded call without the other party's consent is a violation. This legal principle was applied to the monitored Pentagon phone conversation between Senator McCarthy and Secretary Stevens, and underlies arguments about whether subpoenaed monitored calls can be published or entered into evidence without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: FCC rule on use of automatic telephone recording devices
rubrics_metrics.description: When automatic recording machines are used they must emit a 'beep' every 15 seconds to warn the person at the other end of the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FCC requirement for an audible periodic warning applies to automatic devices; a human stenographer taking shorthand notes while listening in is not subject to the 'beep' requirement. This distinction was noted in explaining why the stenographic record of the McCarthy-Stevens call differed from the technical-recording rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate subcommittee subpoena and evidentiary power over monitored conversations
rubrics_metrics.description: A subcommittee motion can call for production of all telephone call records relating to a dispute and may require handing over records among principals; the subcommittee can decide which calls are 'pertinent' and place them into the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News coverage recounts competing positions: some senators/members argued the committee has the power to make monitored conversations part of the record without participants' consent and to decide pertinence; others (and the law quoted above) suggest consent/diffusability limits. The practical guidance from the hearings: committees may subpoena monitored conversations, but legal and fairness objections (and statutory consent requirements for publication) can complicate their admission and public dissemination.
